# New Snack Line for an International Market — First Working Draft

**Circulated for comment, not for approval.** Nothing here needs a decision this week except the three small items in §14. Figures marked *illustrative* are placeholders to be replaced by the Week 6 pack; the reasoning behind them is not a placeholder and is where I would most value being told I am wrong.

*A note on method, offered once: I have taken the liberty of choosing a market rather than presenting a matrix and waiting. The choice is argued in §2 and is designed to be swapped out — the architecture in §3–§7 travels. If the room prefers a different geography, we lose the market data and keep the framework, which seems the cheaper of the two ways to be wrong.*

---

## 0. Executive summary

**The conventional read of the brief.** "Local tastes and eating habits" is usually answered with flavour extensions — take the existing platform, add a local seasoning, print the pack in the local language. That route is fast, cheap, and, on the evidence of most such launches, quietly unsuccessful. Local competitors match a flavour in eight to twelve weeks. Flavour is not defensible.

**The read I would gently put forward instead.** The durable differences between snack markets are not in flavour at all. They are in **occasion, format, price architecture and eating mechanics** — when people snack, how many times a day, with which hand, at what unit price, out of which retail outlet, and whether their fingers can afford to get greasy. Flavour is the entry ticket. Occasion and format are the moat.

**Anchor market proposed: Indonesia.** ~280M people, a median age near 30, and — the number that matters — a snacking frequency (*ngemil*) that in most studies runs to three or four discrete occasions per day, with snacks functioning as partial meal replacement rather than indulgent extras. Two structural features make it unusually attractive to an entrant with a format idea: an extremely granular price ladder starting around Rp 1,000–2,000 (~US$0.06–0.13) that most multinationals find awkward, and a traditional trade of several million *warung* that rewards pack engineering over media spend.

**The line proposed: five platforms, deliberately unequal in risk.**

| | Platform | Bet | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **Wet-spice-paste baked chips** (cassava / taro) — *bumbu*, not powder | Aroma and authenticity at scale | Low |
| **B** | **Tempeh protein crisps** — air-fried, high protein | A local ingredient reframed as functional | Medium |
| **C** | **Dip-and-crunch "wet snack" kits** — *seblak*/*cuanki*-inspired | An eating format no packaged brand owns | High |
| **D** | **Heritage sweets, modernised** — palm sugar, pandan, coconut; sour tropical chews | The under-served afternoon and school occasions | Low–medium |
| **E** | **Gifting and *oleh-oleh* tins** — regional editions, Ramadan hampers | Margin and cultural legitimacy, cheaply bought | Low cost, high seasonality |

**The shape of the ask.** I would rather not ask for a launch budget. I would ask for a small, un-gated sum to run Platform C and one flavour of Platform A into a single city under a **name that is not ours**, through an existing co-packer, inside 14 weeks — and a written stop rule so that failure is cheap and legible rather than defended. Detail in §11 and §14.

---

## 1. How I would suggest this is taken forward

A line like this dies in two ways: by committee dilution before launch, or by being launched at national scale on the strength of a focus group. Both are avoidable.

1. **A small team with real decision rights.** Three or four people — a food technologist, a commercial lead with local trade relationships, a packaging engineer, and someone who can move money — with authority to set recipe, price and pack without sign-off above a defined spend ceiling. Merit, not seniority, on who chairs.
2. **Local hires who can overrule us.** Not advisers. Not a research agency. People with the standing to say "no Indonesian would eat that" and be believed without producing a deck. If we cannot recruit that voice, I would question whether we should enter at all.
3. **A ghost brand.** Launching under an unfamiliar name removes the reputational cost of failure and, more usefully, removes the temptation to defend a poor concept because our logo is on it. It also tells us something honest about whether the product works on its own merits.
4. **Publish what fails.** Including the concepts I am personally attached to. Especially those.
5. **Fewer gates, tighter tripwires.** I would trade three formal stage-gates for one stop rule that fires automatically on a repeat-purchase threshold. The former manages anxiety; the latter manages risk.

The implicit question I would leave with colleagues: *what is the smallest amount of money that would let us find out we are wrong?* Most of this document is an attempt to answer it.

---

## 2. Why this market, and how to substitute it

### 2.1 The case for Indonesia

| Factor | Observation | Why it favours a format-led entrant |
|---|---|---|
| **Snacking frequency** | *Ngemil* is near-continuous; snacks substitute for meals | More occasions to design against; less dependence on one hero SKU |
| **Palate** | Simultaneous heat, sweet, salt and umami; texture prized as much as taste (*kriuk*) | Rewards recipe craft; hard to replicate with a powder dust |
| **Price ladder** | Meaningful volume at Rp 1,000–2,000 single-serve | A pack-engineering problem, which is a competence, not a spend |
| **Channel** | Millions of *warung*; ~45,000 modern-trade minimarkets *(illustrative)* | Hanging *renceng* strips and sachets beat media weight |
| **Digital** | Very high social-commerce and live-selling penetration | A ghost brand can reach scale without distribution first |
| **Seasonality** | Ramadan / Lebaran gifting is an enormous, dateable spike | Platform E buys legitimacy and margin in one move |
| **Regulatory** | Halal certification mandatory; BPOM registration required | A genuine barrier — which cuts both ways, and favours whoever starts the paperwork first |

### 2.2 If the room prefers elsewhere

Offered without argument, so the choice stays open:

- **Vietnam** — younger, faster-growing, strong sour/spicy and dried-fruit heritage; weaker gifting structure.
- **Mexico** — the deepest chilli-lime-and-*salsa* snack culture in the world and the highest per-capita snack spend of the three; also the most saturated and the most defended by incumbents.
- **South Korea** — highest willingness to pay for novelty and the fastest trend cycle globally, which is an opportunity and a treadmill; small population, exportable brand halo.

The occasion-mapping method in §3, the platform architecture in §5 and the test design in §11 apply unchanged to all four. Only §4 and §8 are market-specific.

---

## 3. What we are actually selling: the occasion map

This is the part I would most want challenged, because everything downstream depends on it. The proposition is that we should design **for occasions we can name**, and refuse to launch anything that cannot say which one it serves.

| Occasion | Who / when | Functional demands | Currently served by | Our platform |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **The commute** | Motorcycle and public-transport journeys, twice daily | One-handed; no grease; no shed dust; resealable; survives a bag | Poorly — most chips fail the grease test | A (cluster form), B |
| **Kopi / teh sore** | Late-afternoon coffee or tea, at home or roadside | Sweet-savoury balance; not too filling; shareable | Traditional *kue*, biscuits | D, A |
| **Ngobrol** | Sitting and talking, groups, evenings | Large format; low unit cost; hands-in-bag | Sharing bags, well served | A (100g), C |
| **Late-night gaming / streaming** | 16–28, mostly urban, 21:00–02:00 | Bold heat; substantial; entertaining to eat; photographable | Very poorly — this is the gap | **C** |
| **School and campus** | Rp 1,000–2,000, daily, cash | Absolute price point; sour and spicy skew; peer novelty | Local players own it on price | D (sour chews), A (sachet) |
| **Wellness / gym** | Urban Gen Z, rising fast | Protein claim; "air-fried"; clean label; halal | Imported, expensive, culturally distant | **B** |
| **Buka puasa / takjil** | Ramadan, ~30 dateable evenings | Sweet, dates/palm-sugar register, sharing | Seasonal, fragmented | D, E |
| **Oleh-oleh & Lebaran gifting** | Travel, family visiting, corporate | Presentation; regional identity; premium price tolerance | Fragmented, artisanal, inconsistent | **E** |

Two things I notice, and would be curious whether others read them the same way.

First, the two occasions with the weakest packaged competition — **late-night** and **gifting** — sit at opposite ends of the risk spectrum. That is convenient. One funds the patience needed for the other.

Second, the **commute** occasion is being lost to a manufacturing problem, not a taste problem. Whoever solves shed-dust and finger-grease at the Rp 5,000 price point takes volume without a new flavour idea. That is an unglamorous place to compete, which is generally a good sign.

---

## 4. Flavour architecture

### 4.1 The palate logic

Rather than a flavour list, a small set of rules I would propose we hold ourselves to:

1. **Heat is a ladder, not a level.** Local food culture already numbers its heat (*level 1* to *level 10* in fried-chicken chains). Printing an explicit heat number on pack is culturally native, removes a purchase risk, and lets one recipe base serve three consumer segments. Cheap and, as far as I can find, unclaimed in packaged snacks.
2. **Never heat alone.** The local register is *pedas-manis-asin* — heat carried on sweetness and salt. Heat without sweetness reads as foreign and unfinished.
3. **Aroma is the differentiator, not taste.** Fried shallot, kaffir lime leaf, lemongrass, *terasi*, galangal — these are aroma-forward and largely absent from powder-dusted products because they do not survive spray-drying. This is the technical opening behind Platform A.
4. **Texture is a named benefit.** *Kriuk* — the crunch — should appear on pack and in the product name, not in the fine print.
5. **Sour is under-exploited.** Young mango, *asam*, calamansi, tamarind. Strong in loose/street formats, weak in packaged. Low-cost to test.

### 4.2 Flavour set, by platform

| Platform | Launch flavours | Second wave (validate first) |
|---|---|---|
| A — Wet-spice chips | Sambal matah; Rendang; Sambal ijo | Bumbu Bali; Ayam geprek; Jagung bakar |
| B — Tempeh crisps | Kaldu ayam (chicken broth); Original + sea salt | Black pepper; Cheese; Sambal matah |
| C — Dip-and-crunch | Seblak-style (heat ladder 1/3/5); Cheese-lava | Salted egg (*telur asin*); Tom-yum adjacent |
| D — Sweets | Palm sugar & coconut bites; Pandan; Young-mango sour chew | Kopi susu; Klepon-inspired filled bite |
| E — Gifting | Regional editions built from A and D | Limited spice-region collaborations |

**Cheese and salted egg** deserve a note. Both are enormously popular and both are trend-cycle-dependent. I would carry them as fast-follower SKUs on an existing line rather than as launch propositions — the sort of thing to have ready and hold, not to build a plan around.

---

## 5. The product line

### Platform A — *Bumbu Nyata* (working name): wet-spice-paste baked chips

**The idea.** Cassava (*singkong*) and taro (*talas*) chips, baked or vacuum-fried, tumbled with a **wet spice paste**, not a seasoning powder. Visible spice flecks. Aroma on opening. Formed into small clusters so the seasoning stays on the chip and off the fingers.

**Why it may work.** Every major competitor uses dry powder because powder is stable, cheap and machine-friendly. Wet paste is harder — shorter shelf life, water-activity control, uneven coating risk. That difficulty is precisely the point: it is the one thing in this document a competitor cannot copy in twelve weeks.

**Formats.** 10g sachet (Rp 2,000, sold in hanging *renceng* strips of ten) · 35g (Rp 8,000–10,000, minimarket) · 100g resealable sharing (Rp 22,000–25,000) · e-commerce 6-pack. *All illust
